messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Dat Nguyen had been twenty when he deployed to a conflict zone as a relief worker. The war was a landscape of shifting borders and unpredictable violence. One afternoon, while distributing medical supplies outside a makeshift clinic, the sky fractured with artillery fire. Dat remembered the sudden, suffocating silence that followed, broken only by the crackle of radios and the heavy tread of armed patrols moving through the rubble. He had been pinned under a collapsed awning for hours, unable to move, while soldiers in olive-drab uniforms and heavy tactical vests systematically searched the area, their boots stopping just inches from his face. The unblinking glare of their visored helmets, the sheer weight of their authority, and the terrifying realization that he was entirely at their mercy explained why uniformed presence and the sensation of being watched felt so immediately threatening upon his return. When Dat returned to campus at twenty-two, the quiet rhythm of student life felt fragile. What began as mild startle responses quickly calcified into rigid habits. During an evening seminar, the distant wail of a siren made his breath hitch, and when a campus security officer approached to check on him, the sight of the officer’s navy-blue uniform triggered a sudden, paralyzing urge to flee. He couldn’t help but glance toward the exits, convinced that the authority figure was watching him to single him out. The more Dat felt watched by indifferent crowds or authority figures in police uniforms, the more he convinced himself he couldn't stop bad things from happening to him. He had come to believe he had failed in his most important role in life, and his body kept reacting as if he were still in danger even when he was safe. This conviction of helplessness, paired with the sense of professional inadequacy, sharpened his hypervigilance into a relentless loop. Every time he spotted a police cruiser on the campus perimeter or a military recruiter’s poster on the library stairwell wall, his stomach would knot with dread, which immediately drove him to avoid social contacts with friends he had shared meals with before deployment. He stopped looking people in the eye during hallway encounters, tilting his chin down and gripping his textbook until his knuckles turned white. He avoided the campus safety walkathon entirely when he saw the tactical gear on display, and when a neighboring student reached for a shared textbook, Dat flinched away, unable to tolerate the casual proximity that felt too much like a weapon being brandished. The following months passed in a quiet, self-imposed isolation. His academic workload suffered as he missed seminar discussions, skipping campus events whenever security personnel or campus police were scheduled for safety drills. His body continued to sound alarms long after the war had ended, a constant reminder that he was still unsafe. He would sit in the back of the lecture hall, staring at his laptop screen while his pulse hammered against his ribs, certain that any uniformed presence walking past the glass doors would recognize him as a failure. This interpretation of himself as fundamentally inadequate made every peripheral glance feel like a judgment, which in turn pulled him deeper into social withdrawal. He found himself mapping escape routes before entering any building, his attention fixed on any visual cue of military or police dress that could appear at any moment, convinced that authority presence would inevitably trigger the same paralysis he felt under the awning. The constant dread of being observed, the rigid avoidance of eye contact and pre-trauma social circles, and the exhausting conviction that his body would never stop sounding alarms left him emotionally depleted. What finally brought Dat to the counseling center was a panic attack during a routine orientation briefing, where the sight of a uniformed faculty advisor made him unable to breathe or move. He sat on the floor of the orientation hall, shaking, finally ready to ask for help not because he wanted to relive the past, but because he was terrified that he would never feel safe in his own life again.
